An outie is a type of belly button (also called a navel — the small mark on your stomach) that sticks outward, like a small bump or knob that pokes out from your skin.
Outie vs. Innie — understanding the contrast

Every person has a belly button, but not all belly buttons look the same. They fall into two types:

  • Innie — the belly button curves inward, forming a small pit or hollow. If you poke your finger toward it, it goes into the skin. This is by far the more common type.
  • Outie — the belly button curves or pushes outward, forming a small raised bump that protrudes out of the skin. It looks like a tiny knob sitting on your stomach.

Think of it this way: an innie is like a small bowl pressed into your stomach, while an outie is like a small pea or button sitting on top of it.

When a baby is born, it is connected to its mother through the umbilical cord — a tube that carries food and oxygen from the mother to the baby inside the womb. After birth, this cord is cut. The small leftover piece of cord dries up and naturally falls off within a few weeks, leaving behind the belly button.

How the skin heals and how much scar tissue forms at that spot determines whether the belly button becomes an innie or an outie. An outie simply means a bit more tissue built up during healing, causing that area to push outward instead of folding inward. It has nothing to do with how the cord was cut or tied — it's purely down to how the individual body healed.
Outies are quite rare. The vast majority of people — roughly 90% — have innies. Only about 10% of people (or fewer, by some estimates) have outies, making them noticeably less common.
Is an outie a medical concern?

In almost all cases, no — an outie is completely normal and harmless. It is simply a physical characteristic, like having a certain ear shape or nose shape.

However, in some cases, an outie is caused by a small umbilical hernia — a condition where a tiny bit of soft tissue from inside the abdomen pushes through a small gap in the abdominal muscles at the navel. This sounds alarming, but it is usually harmless. In babies, umbilical hernias almost always close on their own by age 3–4 without any treatment. In adults, if it causes discomfort or grows larger, a doctor may monitor it, though it rarely requires surgery.

So: an outie by itself is just a belly button variation. An outie caused by a hernia is still usually harmless, but worth knowing about.
Does it change with age or body changes?

Sometimes. Pregnant women often find that their innie temporarily becomes an outie as the belly expands and pushes the navel out. It usually returns to its original form after childbirth. Similarly, significant weight gain can sometimes cause a belly button to appear more outie-like, though this is not always permanent.
Any other notable use of "outie" as a noun?

Less commonly, in informal conversation, "outie" can refer to a person who is openly out about something — most often used in LGBTQ+ contexts to refer to someone who is openly out about their identity (as opposed to someone who is not). However, this usage is quite informal and niche. The belly button meaning is by far the most widely recognized and used sense of the noun "outie."

An outie is a belly button that protrudes outward as a small bump, rather than indenting inward. It forms based on how the skin healed after the umbilical cord fell off after birth. It's rare (only about 1 in 10 people have one), completely normal in the vast majority of cases, and carries no medical significance on its own. Its opposite is an innie, which is the far more common type of belly button.
